source.title: DAP: A Discrete-token Autoregressive Planner for Autonomous Driving
source.authors: Bo-Wen Ye; Bin Zhang; Hang Zhao

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports a data-scale sweep for an autonomous-driving planner, a new setting, but does not test language-model loss scaling or fit a power law.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws and uses them as motivation. Its own scaling-related results are PDMS measurements at different training-set sizes; it reports no held-out cross-entropy, power-law fit, exponents, compute sweep, or parameter-count sweep. The cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper cites LM scaling laws (Kaplan, Hoffmann) as motivation for a decoder-only autoregressive driving planner. Its only scaling-related result is a three-point training-set sweep (20k/50k/80k) of a fixed 120M model scored by NAVSIM PDMS, a downstream simulator metric. It has no held-out loss, no power-law fit, no exponents, no compute or parameter sweep, and no extrapolation. Three monotonic points of a downstream score cannot show whether a power-law form holds (V5). V6 concerns language-model downstream predictability, which this does not measure. The finding goes under fits_no_version rather than serving as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right. The authors say the results 'suggest encouraging scaling trends with increased data' and that data scaling is 'effective for this architecture' under ds=16. They also find that coarser ds=32 tokens consistently underperform, and that a larger codebook (C=1024) gives the best PDMS of 90.0. They fit no scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales training-set size for a discrete-token autonomous-driving planner and measures simulator PDMS, rather than fitting language-model held-out cross-entropy laws or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported data-scale outcomes differ by BEV downsampling setting: ds=16 scores exceed ds=32 at corresponding reported sizes.

fits_no_version.finding: For DAP (C=512), NAVSIM v1 PDMS rises monotonically with training-set size from 20k to 50k to 80k. At ds=16 it goes 85.8 to 87.7 to 88.7. At ds=32 the gains are much smaller, 85.7 to 86.1 to 86.4. So the data-scaling benefit depends on the BEV tokenization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a discrete-token driving planner, more training data monotonically improves closed-loop PDMS, with the gain size dependent on tokenization granularity.

record.problems: The data-scale result has only three reported training-set sizes per setting and measures PDMS, not held-out loss. The paper reports no fitted scaling curve or uncertainty for these values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5 also reports a trajectory-only versus joint-supervision/SAC-BC ablation and codebook-size comparisons. These are not data-scale results relevant to the claim and were left out.

untested.parts: No held-out loss and no power-law fit over parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation of parameters versus data.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count.
Driving-planner data scaling is reported, but no power-law form is fitted or tested, and there is no held-out loss.
There is no language-model downstream predictability test. The PDMS sweep has no fitted curve or loss link.
No comparison of fitting choices and no exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation tests/T3 is not supported: the paper cites scaling laws only as motivation, and its sweep is three points of a downstream metric with no fit. Fig. 1b (performance vs model size) compares different published methods, not a controlled parameter sweep, so it should not be a row. The Table 5 C=1024 points (90.0 at ds=16, 86.6 at ds=32, 80k only) were rightly excluded from the data sweep, because codebook size is a separate variable.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss measurements or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions for larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study reports data scaling for an autonomous-driving planner, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in that setting or measure held-out loss.
No test of downstream-task predictability from pretraining loss or a fitted scaling curve.
No comparison of fitting choices, exponents, or departures from a single power law.
